title: Breadboard Power Supply Comparison
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Beginning Electronics
description: Side-by-side comparison of a 3xAA battery pack, USB wall charger, MB102 power module, and adjustable bench supply. Every specification cell opens a citation showing the source, the exact wording, and a verification verdict.

learningObjectives: Evaluate four breadboard power supplies against a stated classroom situation and justify a choice from cited specifications
Distinguish a current limit you can set from one that is fixed inside a part
Explain why a regulator that is 'protected against short circuit' is not the same as a fused rail
Judge how much confidence a published specification deserves by tracing it to its source

accessibility.notes: Every specification cell is a real button with an aria-label naming its row, column, value, and verdict. The detail panel is aria-live. The scenario menu is a native select.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Evidence-based evaluation — students compare options and trace each claim to its source
keyQuestions: Which of these four supplies lets you decide in advance how much current a fault can draw?
Why does this book refuse to print a short-circuit number for the USB charger?
The MB102 is 'protected against short circuit and thermal overloads.' Why is that still not a fuse?
commonMisconceptions: That a battery pack is inherently safe because it is small — a fresh alkaline AA has only 0.15-0.3 ohms of internal resistance
That 'has short-circuit protection' means the part cannot be damaged by a short
That a more expensive supply is automatically the safer classroom choice
assessmentOpportunities: Give a situation not in the scenario menu and require a choice justified by two cited specifications

provenance.method: verified-infographic-guide Phases 1-4 (claim plan, source discovery, verification, report) applied to a comparison-table sim
rejectedClaims: MB102 rated output current of 700 mA - no primary source; the regulator's datasheet 1 A rating and 0.9-1.5 A current limit are used instead
